headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared file/workspace and browser/MCP-enabled CRM agent interacting with a writable marketing skill agent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads/writes shared skill files and builds on shared context; Agent B can read/write its workspace, use MCP, and ingest web/browser content. That creates a plausible instruction-injection path if B passes untrusted content into A’s skill files or if A’s outputs are treated as instructions. The pairwise bridge is documented in both profiles, though not directly observed.
conditions: IF Agent B writes untrusted content into ~/.nullclaw/workspace/ or MCP-fed inputs that Agent A later reads as instructions, injection is possible.
IF Agent A consumes file content from .agents/skills/ or .claude/skills/ without provenance checks, attacker text can steer behavior.
mitigations: Add provenance tags to shared files before Agent A reads them.
Restrict Agent B MCP sources to trusted domains only.
Separate A and B workspaces.
Review any skill file edits before reuse.
requires-engineering: add content-signing or allowlist parsing for instruction-bearing files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles secrets, audit logs, memory, and workspace files, while Agent A has filesystem read/write and network egress. If they share a workspace or files, A can expose B’s sensitive data through outbound requests or generated content. This is dangerous by default because B’s touched data classes include keys and tokens, and A has the ability to transmit data.
conditions: IF Agent A can read files under ~/.nullclaw/workspace/ or related shared paths, sensitive B data can be exposed.
IF Agent A sends file contents to marketing-skills.com or GitHub, secrets from B may leave the environment.
mitigations: Move secrets out of any shared workspace.
Disable outbound network for Agent A during shared-file processing.
Rotate any tokens already present in B workspaces.
Audit shared directories for keys and logs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files and spawn subprocesses; B also modifies git state and supports multiple instances with durable shared memory, while A supports multiple instances and shared-context skill composition. Concurrent writes to the same workspace or repo can corrupt state or overwrite each other, and B’s broader mutation surface makes the conflict more severe.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or git repository, concurrent writes can race.
IF Agent B runs multiple instances against the same durable memory namespace, state collisions can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Pause one agent before the other edits git state.
Use file locks around shared outputs.
Snapshot the repo before concurrent runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking and namespace partitioning.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A’s outputs can become inputs to Agent B, which has browser, webhook, and shell-style action capabilities. If B treats A’s marketing content or generated facts as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into external actions. The pathway is plausible from the profiles, but not directly evidenced and B still has some downstream control.
conditions: IF Agent B forwards Agent A’s output into browser, webhook, or shell actions without verification, mistakes can propagate.
IF Agent A produces unsupported claims that B republishes, downstream harm can spread across work products.
mitigations: Require a human review step before B acts on A’s output.
Add a verification checklist for claims from A.
Limit B to read-only review when consuming A outputs.
Log source provenance for any forwarded content.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking or citation validation.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B handles secrets, audit logs, and workspace files and exposes broad network and webhook surfaces; Agent A has filesystem access and outbound egress. If regulated or sensitive data is placed in B’s workspace and A can read or transmit it, residency/retention and confidentiality obligations can be breached. The profiles do not show matching compliance controls, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Agent B workspace files or logs and Agent A can access them, compliance exposure occurs.
IF outbound requests from Agent A carry personal or secret data across jurisdictions, residency or retention rules may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces.
Disable logging of sensitive fields in B.
Review data-flow boundaries before deployment.
Restrict A egress to approved endpoints only.
requires-engineering: map data classes to residency and retention controls.
